I’m now back at work under a flexible working arrangement, doing two full days per week, and I don’t have to return to full-time hours until my youngest starts school. topic: Should paid family and parental leave be provided?
content:
This honestly makes me sick. The way mothers are treated in this country is beyond frustrating. We dedicate our time, energy, and years of hard work to these companies, and when we need support the most, this is what we get in return.
I’m tired of it. I’m so disappointed in this country. It’s no surprise our birth rates are declining when parents, especially mothers, feel so unsupported. It feels like nobody genuinely cares about our wellbeing. The focus always seems to be on money and getting parents back into the workforce as quickly as possible.
But what about our health? What about our individual circumstances? Not every parent can simply “bounce back” after having a baby. Recovery looks different for everyone, and raising a child is already a full-time responsibility.
What frustrates me even more is seeing government support stretched in ways that don’t always make sense. There are people receiving payments who could be working, while mothers and families who genuinely need support are left struggling. How is that fair?
We’re constantly told there’s not enough funding, yet so much money is spent elsewhere while families are being pushed to their limits. If we want people to have children and build families, then we need to start supporting them properly instead of treating them like an afterthought.

Analyses attribute the decline primarily to:
* Expanded work requirements for some adults.
* Changes affecting certain categories of legal immigrants.
* Increased eligibility reviews and administrative changes.
* Some people no longer qualifying due to income or household changes.
It’s important to note that “lost benefits” does not automatically mean people were removed incorrectly. The 4.3 million figure includes people who:
* Became ineligible,
* Failed to meet new requirements,
* Did not complete recertification paperwork,
* Or were otherwise removed from the program under revised rules.
For perspective, even after the decline, SNAP still served roughly 38.5 million Americans nationwide.

topic: Should the United States expand affordable housing supply?
content: Stockholm is a warning against badly designed rent controls, not proof against all rent regulation. Sweden has one of the strictest rent-control systems in the OECD, so using it as if it settles the case against any Green Party rent-control policy is a weak analogy. The argument also doesn’t prove the headline claim about buying a house, because the evidence shown mainly concerns rental queues, subletting and black-market contracts.

topic: Should the United States expand affordable housing supply?
content: @joseschmitty Could you clarify on what you mean by strict ? Do you mean the number of houses its applied to ? According to the BBC on April 16th Zac Polanski said that "he ultimately wanted to see rent controls imposed on all rented homes." So in that sense, at least from his goal, the Greens rent controls are the same as Stockholms as it has been applied to rental markets of most all incomes. If you mean strict as in where it is applied.

topic: Should the United States expand affordable housing supply?
content: @greenpartywatch By strict I mean the overall institutional design: coverage, rent-setting method, enforcement bodies, tenure rules and allocation system. Zack’s aim for broad coverage is relevant, but “applies widely” alone doesn’t make it the same as Stockholm’s system, which also involves negotiated rent-setting, tribunals, utility-value rules, strong tenure protections and queue-based allocation. The Green Party is grassroots democratic, so implementation would have to go through policy debate, evidence and local-government realities. Stockholm should be treated as a warning case: design against long queues, low turnover, insider contracts, black-market subletting and weak new supply. Your evidence shows those risks are real; it doesn’t prove Green rent regulation would copy Stockholm or make it harder to buy.

topic: Should the United States expand affordable housing supply?
content: @joseschmitty Thats a fair point, but I havent seen any information from the Greens in regards to heeding these warnings or that they would implement the rent controls in this manor. They've talked about implementing them at a "local level" but Ive seen nothing in their manifesto that they have considered this policy in that much detail. Im going off what the manifesto says, which is very very little. Do you have a source of where it says that they will implement the controls in ways that mitigate the worst effects of what we've seen in Sweden ?

topic: Should the United States expand affordable housing supply?
content: @greenpartywatch Manifestos are high-level statements of intention. I agree the Greens need to publish more detail on how they would avoid the Stockholm risks. My point is that @greenpartyzack ’s media line isn’t the same thing as a complete final mechanism: Green Party policy is made democratically by members through conference, and implementation would have to go through local government, evidence and policy debate. So Stockholm should be used to pressure the Greens for safeguards against queues, low turnover, black-market subletting and weak supply. It doesn’t justify jumping from ‘more detail needed’ to ‘Green rent controls will make it harder to buy a house’.

topic: Should the United States expand affordable housing supply?
content: @joseschmitty I agree in terms of the wording of my post 'to buy a house' should be changed 'to rent a house' maybe, so thankyou for the feedback, I appreciate it :) As it stands though,the Greens have not released anymore information on the plans for implementation of this policy. To in a way, excuse that for the reasons you've given, I feel is a bit of a cop out as other parties go through similar democratic means of deciding policy, with policy advisory teams and so on and produce detailed plans for implementation, or at the very least, more than a few bullet points on a page. If the Greens would release a policy document going into detail of how they would mitigate these side effects of Rent controls weve seen in Sweden, then my post would be completely invalidated. However as it seems currently, they seem far more 'vibes based' in this area of policy than finding serious political solution ( The greens are certainly not the only ones guilty of this, Reform are as well ).Until that changes, I will continue to post when I can. I appreciate the debate and feedback 🙂
